Illegality means the state or quality of being against the law. When something violates a rule that is formally established and enforced by a governing authority — a country, a state, a court system — we say it has the quality of illegality. It is the abstract name we give to the condition of being illegal.

Think of it this way: just as "beauty" is the quality of being beautiful, illegality is the quality of being illegal.

This word is actually used in two closely related but different ways, and understanding both is essential.

Meaning 1 — A State or Quality (Abstract)

Here, "illegality" refers to the fact that something breaks the law — it is the name of that legal wrongness itself, not the act.

"The illegality of selling alcohol to minors is well established."

Here, you are not talking about a specific incident. You are talking about the legal status of that action — the fact that the law forbids it. This is illegality used as an idea, a condition, a quality.

More examples:

  • "The illegality of the contract meant it could not be enforced in court." — The contract was void because it violated the law.
  • "The protesters questioned the illegality of the new regulation." — They were challenging whether the regulation truly goes against the law.
  • "She was unaware of the illegality of her actions." — She didn't know that what she was doing was against the law.

In this sense, "illegality" is uncountable — you wouldn't say "an illegality" or "illegalities" when using it this way. You just say "the illegality of something."

Meaning 2 — A Specific Illegal Act (Concrete)

Here, "illegality" refers to an actual act or thing that is illegal — a specific violation of the law. In this use, the word becomes countable, meaning it can take "an" before it and can become plural: illegalities.

"The audit uncovered several illegalities in the company's financial records."

This means the audit found several specific things that violated the law.

More examples:

  • "The politician denied any illegalities in his conduct." — He denied doing anything illegal specifically.
  • "Investigators discovered a string of illegalities at the construction site." — Multiple specific violations of the law were found.
  • "One illegality was enough to get the deal cancelled." — One specific act of breaking the law caused the cancellation.

Think of it like the word "crime." A crime is a specific illegal act. Similarly, an illegality (in this second sense) is a specific thing done that breaks the law.
The Difference Between the Two Meanings — Made Simple

—Meaning 1Meaning 2

Think of it this way. In Meaning 1, you are naming a condition. Like saying "the darkness of the room" — darkness is the condition. You're describing the legal status of something.

In Meaning 2, you are naming a thing that happened. Like saying "there were several crimes" — you are pointing to real acts. You're describing actual violations.

Both meanings are correct and widely used. Context will always make clear which one is intended.

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as understanding what it is.

  • Crime — A crime is a specific act that breaks criminal law and is punishable by the state (imprisonment, fines, etc.). An illegality is broader — it covers any violation of any law, including civil law, regulatory law, and administrative law. So every crime is an illegality, but not every illegality is a crime. For example, a company operating without the correct business license is committing an illegality (it breaks the law), but it may not be a crime in the criminal sense.
  • Wrongdoing — This is a broader, less precise word. Wrongdoing can mean doing something morally wrong, professionally wrong, or legally wrong. Illegality specifically and only refers to legal wrongness. Something can be wrongdoing without being an illegality (e.g., being rude to a colleague), and something can be an illegality without most people considering it "wrong" in a moral sense.
  • Unlawfulness — This is perhaps the closest synonym to "illegality" in Meaning 1. They are nearly interchangeable when describing a state or condition. However, "illegality" is far more commonly used in everyday language, legal writing, and journalism. "Unlawfulness" sounds slightly more formal and technical.
  • Offense / Infraction / Violation — These words name specific acts that break a law or rule, similar to Meaning 2 of illegality. However, they tend to emphasize the act of breaking the rule, while "illegality" emphasizes the legal character of what was done.

When used in Meaning 2 (a specific illegal act), the plural is illegalities. This simply means multiple separate acts that each break the law.

"The investigation revealed a pattern of illegalities spanning several years."

You will see this plural form very commonly in legal, journalistic, and investigative contexts.
Common Patterns You Will See This Word In

Here are the most natural ways "illegality" appears in real usage:

  • "the illegality of [something]" — describing the legal status of an action or situation.
    • "The illegality of insider trading is strictly enforced."
  • "commit / engage in / involve illegalities" — describing specific illegal acts.
    • "The officers were accused of committing illegalities during the search."
  • "alleged illegality" — when someone is accused of something illegal but it hasn't been proven yet.
    • "The report cited alleged illegalities in the bidding process."
  • "question / challenge / dispute the illegality of" — when someone argues that something may actually not be illegal.
    • "The defendant's lawyer challenged the illegality of the evidence obtained."
  • "prove / establish illegality" — when someone must demonstrate in court or officially that something broke the law.
    • "The prosecution must prove illegality beyond a reasonable doubt."
  • "illegality does not excuse [something]" — a common argument that just because one thing is illegal doesn't justify another illegal act in response.

"Illegality" is a formal word. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Legal documents and court proceedings
  • News reporting (especially investigative journalism)
  • Government and policy writing
  • Academic writing (law, political science, social sciences)
  • Formal conversations about rules, laws, and compliance

In everyday casual speech, people more often say "it's illegal" or "that breaks the law" rather than using the word "illegality." But the moment writing or speech becomes formal or official in tone, "illegality" is the natural and precise choice.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

Illegality (noun) has two uses:

  1. The state of being against the law — the abstract quality that makes something illegal.
    • "The illegality of the practice was confirmed by the court."
  2. An actual act that is illegal — a countable, specific violation of the law (plural: illegalities).
    • "The audit exposed multiple illegalities."

It is a formal word, used in legal, journalistic, and official contexts. It is broader than "crime" because it covers all violations of law, not just criminal ones. It is more specific than "wrongdoing" because it refers only to what is legally wrong, not morally wrong.
